records.sourceFile: Cannabis use in adolescent and young adult athletes - A clinical review.pdf

paper.citation: Benoy R, Ramirez C, Hitchcock M, Reardon C. Cannabis use in adolescent and young adult athletes: A clinical review. Sports Health. 2024;16(2):279-284.
paper.abstract: This clinical review examined cannabis prevalence, performance effects, health risks, and regulatory considerations for adolescent and young adult athletes using literature published from 2010 through 2022.
paper.tldr: Survey evidence suggested up to one in four athletes used cannabis in the prior year, while the literature did not support performance enhancement and described objective impairment plus cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, mental-health, and substance-use risks. Product, dose, route, and athlete context vary, so broad claims remain inappropriate.
paper.methods: The authors searched PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and SportDiscus for literature published between January 2010 and December 2022 and added relevant references. The clinical review was classified as level-4 evidence.
paper.findings: Cannabis use varied with age, sex, race, sexual orientation, competition level, and country. Available studies did not support athletic-performance benefit and reported impaired objective performance and potential adverse cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, cognitive, psychiatric, and dependence-related outcomes.
paper.limitations: This was a clinical narrative review rather than a pooled systematic analysis. Much prevalence evidence was self-reported, athlete-specific causal evidence was limited, and cannabis products, THC and CBD content, dosing, routes, and regulatory environments were heterogeneous.
paper.practicalImplications: Ask about cannabis without stigma, distinguish THC from CBD and prescribed medication, and discuss health, cognition, driving, eligibility, and product-contamination risks. Do not endorse cannabis as a performance or recovery intervention from current evidence.
paper.athleteDev: Build pain, sleep, stress, and recovery support around evidence-based training, medical, nutrition, and mental-health care. Young athletes need clear education about brain development, dependence risk, and team or anti-doping rules.
paper.rtp: Acute intoxication, withdrawal, mental-health symptoms, or cardiovascular effects can compromise safe participation. Return decisions require clinical assessment and functional readiness, not simply elapsed time since reported use.

records.sourceFile: Basal Serum Cortisol and   Testosterone-Cortisol Ratio Are Related to Rate of Na+ Lost During  Exercise  in Elite Soccer Players.pdf

paper.citation: Castro-Sepulveda M, Cancino J, Fernández-Verdejo R, et al. Basal serum cortisol and testosterone/cortisol ratio are related to rate of Na+ lost during exercise in elite soccer players. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2019;29(6):658-663.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study examined whether basal testosterone, cortisol, or their ratio was related to sweat sodium-loss rate during one training session in 22 elite male soccer players.
paper.tldr: Higher basal cortisol was associated with greater sodium-loss rate and a higher testosterone-to-cortisol ratio with lower loss, independent of sweat rate. These modest correlations do not establish causality, the proposed transport mechanism, or a hormone-based sodium prescription.
paper.methods: Basal serum testosterone and cortisol were measured before exercise. Sweat samples and sweat rate were collected during training, sodium-loss rate was calculated, and associations were examined while accounting for sweating rate.
paper.findings: Sodium-loss rate correlated positively with cortisol at r=.43 and negatively with the testosterone-to-cortisol ratio at r=-.46. The study proposed possible regulation through the cystic-fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator but did not test that pathway.
paper.limitations: The sample included only 22 elite men and one training exposure. Cross-sectional correlations are sensitive to hormonal, dietary, environmental, acclimation, and measurement variation and cannot define individual replacement needs or prove a biological mechanism.
paper.practicalImplications: When sodium replacement precision matters, measure individual sweat rate and sweat sodium under representative conditions. Do not substitute basal hormone testing for direct sweat assessment.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes to individualize fluid and sodium plans for duration, climate, acclimation, and known sweat losses. Reassess across materially different environments rather than relying on a permanent label.
paper.rtp: Hormone values from this study do not determine readiness. During heat, illness, or heavy training, use symptoms, hydration status, environmental exposure, medical context, and a progressive return plan.

records.sourceFile: Change of Direction Deficit vs Deceleration Deficit - A Comparison of Limb Dominance and Inter limb Asymmetry between Forwards and Backs in Elite Male Rugby Union Players.pdf

paper.citation: Bishop C, Clarke R, Freitas TT, et al. Change-of-direction deficit vs. deceleration deficit: A comparison of limb dominance and inter-limb asymmetry between forwards and backs in elite male rugby union players. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2021;39(10):1088-1095.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study compared change-of-direction and deceleration deficits, limb dominance, asymmetry, jumping, and speed in 25 elite male rugby-union players at the end of preseason.
paper.tldr: Change-of-direction and deceleration tests produced only moderate agreement on limb dominance, and asymmetry direction varied across tasks. Deficit and asymmetry scores also related weakly to general jump and speed performance, so these measures are not interchangeable athlete traits.
paper.methods: Players completed bilateral jump, linear-speed, 505 change-of-direction, and deceleration tests. Left- and right-side deficits, asymmetry, limb-dominance agreement, correlations, and forward-versus-back differences were calculated.
paper.findings: Dominance agreement between change-of-direction and deceleration deficits was moderate. Jump and linear or change-of-direction speed relationships were moderate to large, but deficit and asymmetry relationships were small. Backs were faster over 15 m and performed better in most jump tests than forwards.
paper.limitations: The sample was small, male, elite, rugby-specific, and assessed at one time point. Test-specific calculations, no prospective injury or performance outcomes, and no intervention or between-session reliability analysis prevent stable labeling or causal interpretation.
paper.practicalImplications: Choose a test that matches the decision and preserve its exact setup. Interpret change-of-direction, stopping, and limb outputs separately and confirm unexpected findings across repeated representative tasks.
paper.athleteDev: Develop acceleration, braking, reacceleration, and directional skill while accounting for position demands. Avoid building a program around a favored limb that changes with the task.
paper.rtp: Track repeatable performance in the exact change-of-direction and deceleration tasks relevant to reintegration. Clearance should include symptoms, absolute capacity, movement quality, directional variety, fatigue, and rugby exposure.

records.sourceFile: Comparisons of new body load and metabolic power average workload indices between starters and non-starters - A full-season study in professional soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Nobari H, Praça GM, Clemente FM, et al. Comparisons of new body load and metabolic power average workload indices between starters and non-starters: A full-season study in professional soccer players. Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers, Part P: Journal of Sports Engineering and Technology. 2021;235(2):105-113.
paper.abstract: This full-season observational study compared body-load- and metabolic-power-derived weekly training monotony and strain between starters and nonstarters in 21 professional Iranian Premier League soccer players.
paper.tldr: Starters showed very large higher derived monotony and strain values than nonstarters in early, mid, and end-season periods, largely reflecting match exposure. The one-team data identify workload divergence but do not validate the indices as readiness or injury-risk measures.
paper.methods: Players wore GPS devices throughout the season and were classified weekly according to match and training participation. New body load and average metabolic power were used to calculate weekly monotony and strain across preseason and three in-season periods.
paper.findings: Starters had very large higher values across all four indices in early, mid, and end season, with standardized differences generally above 2.4 and reaching 3.58. The groups did not show the same clear pattern during preseason.
paper.limitations: The study involved one small team, weekly changing group membership, repeated observations, and proprietary derived variables. It did not test injury, recovery, performance, or whether manipulating the reported indices improves outcomes.
paper.practicalImplications: Use match participation to anticipate divergent exposure and compare starters and nonstarters across the actual underlying load measures. Avoid red-light decisions or injury claims from derived monotony and strain values alone.
paper.athleteDev: Provide nonstarters with planned exposure that preserves relevant running and mechanical qualities while managing the greater match-driven load of starters. Individual response should determine the adjustment.
paper.rtp: Use the athlete's accumulating training and match exposure to plan reintegration, but do not equate a target monotony or strain score with readiness. Pair load with symptoms, function, and recovery response.

records.sourceFile: Cutoffs of isokinetic strength      ratio and hamstring strain prediction in professional soccer   players.pdf

paper.citation: Dauty M, Menu P, Fouasson-Chailloux A. Cutoffs of isokinetic strength ratio and hamstring strain prediction in professional soccer players. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2018;28(1):276-281.
paper.abstract: This prospective cohort analysis tested whether preseason bilateral, conventional, or functional isokinetic knee-strength-ratio cutoffs predicted moderate hamstring strain in 194 professional soccer players observed across 15 seasons.
paper.tldr: Thirty-six players sustained hamstring strain, but neither common published cutoffs nor cohort-specific 10th-percentile cutoffs predicted injury. Isokinetic testing can describe strength capacity; converting ratios into binary injury-risk labels was not supported.
paper.methods: Bilateral concentric and eccentric hamstring ratios, conventional hamstring-to-quadriceps ratios, and mixed functional ratios were calculated at preseason. Multiple published cutoffs and cohort-derived cutoffs were tested with odds ratios against subsequent injury.
paper.findings: No bilateral, conventional, or functional cutoff predicted hamstring strain in univariate analysis. Very few injured players fell below some commonly used thresholds, and population-specific thresholds were not more successful.
paper.limitations: Only 36 injuries occurred, data spanned 15 seasons, and strength ratios depend on testing velocity, contraction mode, equipment, and protocol. Injury is multifactorial, and failure of cutoffs does not mean absolute hamstring strength or repeated testing lacks clinical value.
paper.practicalImplications: Stop using one preseason isokinetic ratio as a hamstring-injury prediction test. Review absolute knee-flexor capacity, exposure, prior injury, sprint preparation, symptoms, and change over time together.
paper.athleteDev: Train hamstring strength across relevant lengths, velocities, and functions and maintain high-speed-running exposure. Aim to improve capacity rather than merely cross an unvalidated ratio threshold.
paper.rtp: Ratios may supplement side-specific capacity assessment after injury, but clearance should not depend on a cutoff. Include absolute strength, symptoms, sprint progression, fatigue tolerance, and football-specific exposure.

records.sourceFile: Muscle activity and kinematics during three hamstring strengthening exercises compared to sprinting - A cross-sectional study.pdf

paper.citation: Jorge A, Lichtenstein E, Faude O, Roth R. Muscle activity and kinematics during three hamstring strengthening exercises compared to sprinting: A cross-sectional study. International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy. 2024;19(5):569-580.
paper.abstract: This laboratory study compared hamstring and posterior-chain surface electromyography and lower-limb kinematics during three hip-dominant exercises, Nordic hamstring exercise, and treadmill running in eight healthy male athletes.
paper.tldr: Explosive rocker and fast-perpetuum-mobile variants generated the greatest hamstring activity, but every exercise reached peak activity at shorter hamstring lengths than high-speed running. High activation can complement sprint preparation but does not reproduce sprint mechanics or prove injury prevention.
paper.methods: Surface electromyography measured biceps femoris, semitendinosus, gluteus maximus, and medial gastrocnemius activity, normalized to maximal sprinting. Three-dimensional motion capture compared joint angles during exercises and treadmill running at 75% of maximal sprint velocity.
paper.findings: Hamstring activity ranged from 63.9% of normalized sprint values for the rocker to 32.1% for the slow perpetuum-mobile exercise. Biceps femoris activity exceeded semitendinosus across exercises, while all exercise peaks occurred with less hamstring elongation stress than running.
paper.limitations: Only eight healthy men participated. Surface electromyography is not direct muscle force, treadmill running at 75% differs from maximal field sprinting, and the cross-sectional study did not measure adaptation, injury, soreness, or program effectiveness.
paper.practicalImplications: Select exercises by the joint, speed, muscle-length, and activation stimulus required. Combine strength work with progressive sprint exposure rather than choosing exercises solely because an electromyographic value is high.
paper.athleteDev: Use multiple hamstring strategies across hip- and knee-dominant patterns, tempos, and lengths, then integrate high-speed running. Progress load based on technique and tolerance.
paper.rtp: Exercise activity data can guide early and middle rehabilitation loading, but sprint-specific length and speed demands must be restored separately before unrestricted return.

records.sourceFile: A qualitative study of 11 world-class team sport athletes' experiences answering subjective questionnairs - A key ingredient for visible health and performance monitoring.pdf

paper.citation: McCall A, Wolfberg A, Ivarsson A, et al. A qualitative study of 11 world-class team-sport athletes' experiences answering subjective questionnaires: A key ingredient for visible health and performance monitoring? Sports Medicine. 2023;53(5):1085-1100.
paper.abstract: This phenomenological qualitative study explored why 11 world-class team-sport athletes were or were not honest when answering subjective health and performance questionnaires.
paper.tldr: Athlete disclosure was shaped by pursuit of an ideal self, personal barriers, social facilitators, and perceived compassion from staff. Subjective-monitoring quality is partly a relationship and system-design problem, not simply athlete compliance.
paper.methods: Five women and six men were interviewed about monitoring experiences. Researchers extracted significant statements, formulated meanings, coded categories, developed themes, and created a blended thematic story across athlete accounts.
paper.findings: Four themes emerged: pursuit of the ideal self, individual barriers to engagement, social facilitators, and feeling compassion from performance staff. Athlete emotions and the behavior of staff asking the questions influenced willingness to disclose honestly.
paper.limitations: The small purposive elite sample and qualitative interpretation cannot estimate how common a behavior is, validate a questionnaire, or prove that a specific staff intervention changes response accuracy. Findings are context dependent.
paper.practicalImplications: Explain why data are collected, respond consistently and compassionately, protect appropriate confidentiality, and demonstrate that honest answers lead to useful support rather than punishment. Review the workflow when responses appear unreliable.
paper.athleteDev: Build athlete agency and communication skills alongside self-awareness. Monitoring should create a safe conversation and shared decision surface, not a surveillance exercise.
paper.rtp: Subjective readiness is valuable when trust permits honest disclosure, but it should be combined with clinical findings, functional testing, load tolerance, and the athlete's informed voice.

records.sourceFile: Pectoralis Major ruptures during rugby league tackling – case series with implications for tackling technique instruction .pdf

paper.citation: Sartori S, Whiteley R. Pectoralis major ruptures during rugby league tackling: Case series with implications for tackling technique instruction. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2019;22(12):1298-1303.
paper.abstract: This retrospective case series described three complete pectoralis-major ruptures sustained while tackling by players from one 36-man professional rugby-league squad during the same season.
paper.tldr: All three injuries occurred with the shoulder in outer-range abduction and horizontal abduction during contact after a defensive approach change. Each player underwent acute repair and returned at the same level, but three clustered cases cannot prove that the technique change caused the injuries.
paper.methods: The authors reviewed the injury mechanisms, squad incidence, treatment, and outcomes of three professional players and compared the cluster with available literature. Tackle position and organizational context were reconstructed for each case.
paper.findings: The three players appeared to tear the pectoralis major while attempting the tackle from a similar vulnerable shoulder position. Acute surgical management was used in all cases, and each returned to play at the prior level.
paper.limitations: This uncontrolled three-case series from one squad and season cannot estimate causal risk or separate technique, exposure, strength, fatigue, individual anatomy, and chance. The mechanism assessment was observational and retrospective.
paper.practicalImplications: When changing tackle technique, introduce it progressively, monitor unintended exposures, and coordinate coaching, medical, and performance feedback. Prepare shoulder and pectoral capacity for the positions the new technique creates.
paper.athleteDev: Develop contact skill and shoulder-girdle capacity together, particularly for outer-range force acceptance. Technical changes require rehearsal and progressive collision exposure rather than verbal instruction alone.
paper.rtp: The cases returned after surgical repair, but the series does not define a timeline or clearance test. Restore healing, strength through range, contact mechanics, confidence, and progressive tackle exposure.

records.sourceFile: Practices and perceptions in hamstring training for injury prevention and enhancement of athletic performance - A qualitative analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Ross S, Ripley NJ, Comfort P. Practices and perceptions in hamstring training for injury prevention and enhancement of athletic performance: A qualitative analysis. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2025:17479541251374792.
paper.abstract: This qualitative study interviewed 12 strength-and-conditioning and physiotherapy practitioners to understand how hamstring-injury-prevention and performance research is translated into applied programs.
paper.tldr: Limited athlete contact, fixture congestion, and multidisciplinary planning constrained practice; microdosing and isometrics were common adaptations. Some low-volume Nordic and minimum-effective-dose findings were not consistently translated, highlighting an implementation and communication gap rather than proof of one best method.
paper.methods: Semi-structured interviews covered practitioner role, job constraints, resistance training, high-speed running, testing and monitoring, and views of research. Thematic analysis identified shared challenges, strategies, and evidence-to-practice gaps.
paper.findings: Practitioners described time, schedules, and multidisciplinary coordination as major constraints. They used microdosed resistance work and isometrics during congestion, while calling for better education, team planning, and research on minimum effective strength doses.
paper.limitations: The purposive sample was small and mixed across sports and roles. Self-reported perceptions do not establish intervention efficacy, prevalence, adherence, or athlete outcomes, and qualitative themes depend partly on researcher interpretation.
paper.practicalImplications: Plan hamstring exposure across the multidisciplinary team, protect a minimum effective stimulus during congestion, and document what is actually delivered. Distinguish evidence, local constraints, and practitioner preference.
paper.athleteDev: Maintain year-round hamstring strength and sprint exposure with doses that fit the calendar. Education and athlete buy-in help preserve consistency when full sessions are not possible.
paper.rtp: Rehabilitation and team training should share a clear progression for strength, running speed, volume, and role demands. Practitioner consensus alone should not determine clearance.

records.sourceFile: The safety of blood flow restriction training as a therapeutic intervention for patients with musculoskleletal disorders - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Minniti MC, Statkevich AP, Kelly RL, et al. The safety of blood flow restriction training as a therapeutic intervention for patients with musculoskeletal disorders: A systematic review. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;48(7):1773-1785.
paper.abstract: This systematic review summarized adverse-event reporting from 19 blood-flow-restriction-training studies involving 322 people with musculoskeletal disorders.
paper.tldr: Fourteen adverse events were reported: 10 among 168 blood-flow-restriction participants and four among 154 controls. Three rare events in blood-flow-restriction groups included deep-vein thrombosis and rhabdomyolysis; the evidence was mostly knee related and safety reporting was incomplete, so the intervention appears feasible but not risk free.
paper.methods: MEDLINE, CINAHL, and Embase were searched for human musculoskeletal studies using blood-flow restriction that addressed adverse events. Diagnoses, protocols, common and rare events, and randomized comparisons were synthesized.
paper.findings: Nine studies reported no adverse events. Randomized trials did not show a higher overall event likelihood than exercise alone, while three rare events and several episodes of acute pain or fatigue were documented. Many otherwise eligible studies were excluded because safety was not reported.
paper.limitations: Samples were small, diagnoses and protocols varied, adverse-event definitions were inconsistent, and evidence concentrated on knee disorders. Nonreporting can hide events, and the review could not establish safety for every diagnosis, vascular-risk profile, cuff, or occlusion pressure.
paper.practicalImplications: Use medical screening, individualized arterial-occlusion pressure, appropriate cuffs and loads, supervision, symptom education, and explicit adverse-event documentation. Stop and assess concerning pain, neurologic, vascular, or systemic symptoms.
paper.athleteDev: Blood-flow restriction can provide a lower-load strength stimulus when heavier loading is not tolerated, but it should transition into broader capacity development as appropriate rather than replace conventional training indefinitely.
paper.rtp: Use blood-flow restriction as one rehabilitation tool under qualified supervision, not as a clearance test. Progress tissue loading, absolute strength, function, and sport exposure while accounting for contraindications and adverse response.

records.sourceFile: A systematic review of resistance training methodogies for the development of lower body concentric mean power, peak power, and mean propulsive power in team-sport athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Cormier P, Freitas TT, Seaman K. A systematic review of resistance training methodologies for the development of lower body concentric mean power, peak power, and mean propulsive power in team-sport athletes. Sports Biomechanics. 2024;23(10):1229-1262.
paper.abstract: This systematic review evaluated 19 studies of resistance-training methods intended to improve lower-body concentric mean, peak, or mean-propulsive power in team-sport athletes and considered their seasonal implementation.
paper.tldr: Traditional strength and combination methods had the strongest evidence, with support for optimal-load and velocity-based training when monitoring was available. Flywheel, eccentric-overload, and weightlifting methods were also favorable but backed by fewer studies; no single method was universally superior.
paper.methods: The authors extracted baseline-to-post percentage change, effect sizes, and evidence level for power outcomes. Methods included traditional, complex, contrast, optimal-load, velocity-based, flywheel, eccentric-overload, and weightlifting approaches.
paper.findings: Traditional and combination training were supported by higher-level evidence. Optimal-load and velocity-based approaches were practical when movement velocity and power could be monitored, while several specialized methods showed promise with lower evidence certainty.
paper.limitations: The 19 studies varied in athlete level, sport, training history, power metric, device, duration, and reporting of concurrent sport load. Some methods had few studies, and the review did not identify one optimal method or annual plan for all team sports.
paper.practicalImplications: Choose the simplest method that targets the athlete's power limitation and fits the calendar, coaching expertise, and available measurement. Track actual load, velocity, and adaptation rather than following a method label.
paper.athleteDev: Build a strength foundation, then expose athletes to force- and velocity-oriented power work across the year. Adjust volume during congested technical and competition periods while preserving enough stimulus to maintain power.
paper.rtp: Power training can support late-stage rehabilitation after sufficient tissue and strength preparation. Progress force, velocity, landing, and sport-specific expression; do not use a program category as a clearance criterion.
